entries.lesson_core_move: State the convolution theorem as the operational equivalence between continuous-time convolution and Fourier-domain multiplication, connecting direct LTI output convolution to frequency-domain signal analysis.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Convolution Theorem

blocks.text: When an LTI output is written as $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$, the convolution theorem tells you how to read its Fourier-domain form: the output spectrum is the product $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.

This is the same system described two ways. On the time-domain side, the input and impulse response combine by convolution; on the frequency-domain side, their spectra combine by multiplication. The theorem gives the matching between those two descriptions.

So the operational rule is: if you know the LTI output in the form $x(t)*h(t)$, you can move to frequency analysis by taking the Fourier transform and replacing convolution with multiplication of spectra.
In the next sections, you will use this notation to recognize each side separately and connect the theorem back to LTI output analysis.

sections.section_title: Recognizing the Time-Domain Convolution Side

example_content.example_prompt: Given $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$, identify the operation and rewrite it in compact convolution notation.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the standard convolution pattern: one factor is written as $x(\tau)$, the other is shifted to $h(t-\tau)$, and the whole expression is integrated over $\tau$ to produce $y(t)$.
That pattern is the time-domain side of the theorem, so the operation is convolution. In compact notation, rewrite the output as $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$.
This is the notation the rest of the topic will reuse whenever an LTI output is being described in the time domain.

sections.section_title: Stating the Matching Fourier-Domain Product

example_content.example_prompt: If $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$, write the Fourier-domain expression for the output spectrum.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the time-domain output written in convolution form as $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$. That tells you to apply the convolution theorem to the output, not to introduce a new operation.

By the theorem, the Fourier-domain version of that same LTI output is the product of the input and impulse-response spectra. Keep the transformed output label on the left and the two spectra on the right.

So the matching frequency-domain statement is $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$, which is the form the rest of the topic will use when it shifts from time-domain convolution to frequency-domain analysis.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the Theorem as an LTI Output Relationship

example_content.example_prompt: For an LTI system with input $x(t)$ and impulse response $h(t)$, explain what the theorem says about the output in the time and frequency domains.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is one LTI system described by its input $x(t)$ and impulse response $h(t)$. The theorem says to describe that same output in both the time domain and the frequency domain.

Those two lines are not two different outputs. The first line is the time-domain view, where the output is obtained by convolution, and the second line is the frequency-domain view, where the output spectrum is the product of the input and impulse-response spectra.

So the theorem is an output relationship: use the time-domain form when direct output computation is the goal, and use the frequency-domain form when spectral analysis is the clearer way to read the same system.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert y(t)=x(t)*h(t) into Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega) to represent a convolution-based LTI system output in the Fourier domain.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Fourier Transform of a Convolution

blocks.text: When an LTI output is written as $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$, the Fourier-transform label for that output is $Y(j\omega)$. Read $Y(j\omega)$ as the output spectrum of the same signal, not as a new signal.

To move from the time domain to the frequency domain, apply the convolution theorem to that same output. The output spectrum is still labeled $Y(j\omega)$, and it matches the product form of the input and impulse-response spectra.

So the same LTI output has two matching views: the time-domain convolution $y(t)$ and the Fourier-domain spectrum $Y(j\omega)$. The spectrum keeps the output label and simply changes the representation.

In later sections, you will read the same mapping from equivalent convolution forms, including reversed factors and the expanded convolution integral. The rule stays the same: convolution in time becomes multiplication in frequency.

sections.section_title: Transforming y(t)=x(t)*h(t) into the Output Spectrum

example_content.example_prompt: Given an LTI output $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$, write the Fourier-domain expression for $Y(j\omega)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the convolution form $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$. Since the output is already written as an LTI convolution, the right move is to read it in the Fourier domain.
Applying the convolution theorem keeps the same output label and turns the time-domain output into the product of the input and impulse-response spectra. The Fourier-domain output is $Y(j\omega)$.
So the transformed output is $Y(j\omega)$, and its frequency-domain form is exactly the product $X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$. That is the Fourier-domain representation of the same LTI output.

sections.section_title: Transforming h(t)*x(t) into the Same Product Spectrum

example_content.example_prompt: Given $y(t)=h(t)*x(t)$, write the Fourier transform of the output.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the reversed convolution order $y(t)=h(t)*x(t)$. Because convolution is commutative, this is the same LTI output written with the factors swapped.
Apply the same convolution theorem to the reordered output. The Fourier-domain output label stays $Y(j\omega)$, and the spectrum is still the product of the input and impulse-response spectra.
So swapping the order of the time-domain factors does not change the output spectrum. The same LTI output is still represented by the product $X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ in the Fourier domain.

sections.section_title: Transforming a Convolution Integral into a Product Spectrum

example_content.example_prompt: Given $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$, write the Fourier-domain expression for the output.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the integral form of the output: it already matches the standard convolution pattern with $x(\tau)$ and $h(t-\tau)$.
Read that integral as $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$, then apply the convolution theorem to move the same output into the Fourier domain.
The result is the product spectrum for the same LTI output, now represented by $Y(j\omega)$.

sections.section_title: Identifying X(j\omega)H(j\omega) as the Fourier Transform of x(t)*h(t)

example_content.example_prompt: Given $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$, identify the corresponding time-domain output $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the product spectrum $X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$. Read that product as the Fourier-domain form of a convolution output, not as pointwise multiplication in time.
So the matching time-domain signal is the LTI output $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$. This is the same output written in the time domain instead of the Fourier domain.
The product spectrum and the convolution output are two views of the same system response.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the pointwise product X(j\omega)H(j\omega) and interpret its magnitude and phase as the Fourier-domain representation of the time-domain convolution x(t)*h(t).

sections.section_title: Introduction to Multiplication in the Frequency Domain

blocks.text: For an LTI output written as $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$, the Fourier-domain rule is $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$. Read it one frequency at a time: at each fixed $\omega$, multiply the two complex values.
That product is the frequency-domain form of the same output, not a new time-domain operation. The move in this lesson is to replace the convolution with pointwise multiplication of the spectra.
When each factor is written in polar form, the magnitude and phase of the product are visible immediately.
So the output spectrum is built frequency by frequency, and the next sections will use the same rule to read the product, its magnitude, its phase, and its meaning as the spectrum of $x(t)*h(t)$.

sections.section_title: Pointwise Multiplication of X(j\omega) and H(j\omega)

example_content.example_prompt: Given $X(j\omega)=2e^{j\pi/6}e^{-j\omega/2}$ and $H(j\omega)=3e^{-j\pi/3}e^{j\omega}$, compute $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ and simplify the result.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the pointwise product: keep the same $\omega$ and multiply the two spectra directly. Start by writing $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.
Multiply the magnitudes first: $2\cdot 3=6$. Then combine the exponential factors by adding the constant phase terms and the $\omega$-dependent terms.
So the simplified spectrum is $Y(j\omega)=6e^{j(\omega/2-\pi/6)}$. The magnitude is $6$, and the phase is $\omega/2-\pi/6$.

sections.section_title: Magnitude of a Frequency-Domain Product

example_content.example_prompt: Using the same $X(j\omega)=2e^{j\pi/6}e^{-j\omega/2}$ and $H(j\omega)=3e^{-j\pi/3}e^{j\omega}$, find $|Y(j\omega)|$ for $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is magnitude only, so use the product rule for magnitudes: $|Y(j\omega)|=|X(j\omega)H(j\omega)|=|X(j\omega)|\,|H(j\omega)|$.
Each complex exponential has unit magnitude, so the phase factors do not change the size of the product. Only the real coefficients remain.
So the magnitude of the frequency-domain product is constant: $|Y(j\omega)|=6$.

sections.section_title: Phase of a Frequency-Domain Product

example_content.example_prompt: Using the same $X(j\omega)=2e^{j\pi/6}e^{-j\omega/2}$ and $H(j\omega)=3e^{-j\pi/3}e^{j\omega}$, find $\angle Y(j\omega)$ for $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is phase, so read the argument of each factor and add them pointwise in $\omega$. The positive coefficients $2$ and $3$ contribute no phase.
Now add the phase terms from the two spectra. Keep the dependence on $\omega$ together and simplify the constant offset.
So the phase of the frequency-domain product is $\angle Y(j\omega)=\omega/2-\pi/6$.

sections.section_title: Reading X(j\omega)H(j\omega) as the Spectrum of x(t)*h(t)

example_content.example_prompt: Given the product $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$, identify the corresponding time-domain output $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$ and state what the product means in the Fourier domain.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is interpretation: the same pointwise product in frequency is the spectrum of the convolution output in time.
So $Y(j\omega)$ is not a time-domain product or a sum. It is the Fourier-domain representation of $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$, and its magnitude and phase describe that output spectrum.
That compact product is the spectrum of the convolution output, so the earlier magnitude and phase results are now read as features of $x(t)*h(t)$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compare y(t)=x(t)*h(t) with Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega) by deciding which domain gives the clearer computation or interpretation of an LTI system output.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Time-Domain Convolution vs. Frequency-Domain Multiplication

blocks.text: The same continuous-time LTI output can be written in two equivalent forms. In the time domain, it appears as the convolution of the input $x(t)$ with the impulse response $h(t)$. In the frequency domain, it appears as the product of their spectra. This step is only about recognizing which form makes the task easier.
Use the time domain when the question is about overlap, support, shifting, or the geometry of the convolution integral. Those features are easiest to see before transforming anything.

Use the frequency domain when the question is about algebraic combination, spectrum shaping, or the interpretation of the output spectrum. Multiplication is the direct operation in that representation.

The decision rule is simple: choose the domain that exposes the feature the question is asking about. For this lesson, the goal is to recognize the two equivalent forms and decide which one gives the clearer computation or interpretation.

sections.section_title: Matching y(t)=x(t)*h(t) with Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)

example_content.example_prompt: Match the time-domain output $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$ to its frequency-domain form $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ and name which factors come from the input and impulse response.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the output written as $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$. That tells you the time-domain form is a convolution of the input and the impulse response, so the output is being described before any transformation.

The matching frequency-domain form is $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$. Here the output spectrum is the product of the input spectrum and the impulse-response spectrum, so convolution in time becomes multiplication in frequency.

So the symbols line up as $x(t)\leftrightarrow X(j\omega)$, $h(t)\leftrightarrow H(j\omega)$, and $y(t)\leftrightarrow Y(j\omega)$. The same LTI output is being written in two different domains, and the frequency-domain version keeps the output as a simple product.

sections.section_title: Choosing Time-Domain Convolution for Overlap and Support Questions

example_content.example_prompt: For finite-duration signals such as $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$ and $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-1)$, decide whether the time domain is the clearest route and determine the support of $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is finite-duration pulses and a question about support and overlap. That makes this a time-domain signal-shape problem, so the first move is to slide one pulse across the other instead of trying to reason from spectra first.

Here $x(t)$ is nonzero on $0 \le t < 2$ and $h(t)$ is nonzero on $0 \le t < 1$. When one pulse is shifted across the other, the output is nonzero exactly while their intervals overlap, so the support comes straight from the geometry of the two finite intervals.

So the time domain is the clearest route here. You do not need spectral algebra to answer the support question: the overlap starts at $t=0$ and ends after the combined pulse widths have passed, so $y(t)$ is supported on $0 \le t \le 3$.

sections.section_title: Choosing Frequency-Domain Multiplication for Algebraic Computation

example_content.example_prompt: For spectra such as $X(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega}$ and $H(j\omega)=\frac{2}{1-j\omega}$, decide whether the frequency domain is the clearer route and compute $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that both inputs are already given as algebraic spectra. That makes the frequency domain the clearest route, because the output spectrum is obtained by direct multiplication instead of by setting up a time-domain convolution integral.
Now multiply the factors and simplify the denominator. The algebra stays compact, which is exactly why the frequency domain is the better choice for this kind of input.

So the result follows immediately from the product rule: $Y(j\omega)$ is just the simplified product of $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$. In this setting, time-domain convolution would add unnecessary work without making the answer clearer.

sections.section_title: Choosing the Clearer Domain for Interpreting an LTI Output

example_content.example_prompt: An input $x(t)$ has several frequency components and $H(j\omega)$ strongly attenuates the high-frequency components. Decide which domain is clearer for interpreting the output and explain what the product $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ says about $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is not a computation request but an interpretation request about filtering. That makes the frequency domain the clearest choice, because it shows directly which parts of the spectrum are passed and which parts are suppressed.

Because $H(j\omega)$ is small at high $|\omega|$, the high-frequency components of $X(j\omega)$ are reduced in the product. The low-frequency parts survive more strongly, so the spectrum of the output is shaped by the filter rather than by a time-domain overlap picture.

So the frequency domain gives the clearest interpretation: $y(t)$ is the waveform whose spectrum keeps the low-frequency content and suppresses the high-frequency content. In this kind of question, the product rule explains the output more directly than time-domain convolution does.

entries.lesson_title: Proof Idea of the Convolution Theorem
entries.lesson_core_move: Trace the proof idea of the convolution theorem by substituting the convolution integral into the Fourier transform definition, interchanging integration order, and recognizing the two individual spectra.

sections.lesson_title: Proof Idea of the Convolution Theorem
sections.section_title: Introduction to Proof Idea of the Convolution Theorem

blocks.text: Start with one continuous-time LTI output, written as $y(t)=(x*h)(t)$. The target is to rewrite its Fourier transform until it becomes $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.
The other ingredient is the Fourier transform definition of the output spectrum, $Y(j\omega)$. These two formulas are the only pieces needed before the algebra begins.

The proof path is symbolic: substitute the convolution integral into the transform definition, rewrite the result as a double integral, swap the order of integration, and then recognize the factors that depend only on $t$ or $\tau$.
Keep the focus on the proof idea rather than on formal convergence details. The next step will begin the algebraic rewrite immediately.

sections.lesson_title: Proof Idea of the Convolution Theorem
sections.section_title: Substituting the Convolution Integral into the Fourier Transform

example_content.example_prompt: Start from $Y(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(x*h)(t)e^{-j\omega t}\,dt$ and substitute the convolution definition for $(x*h)(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the convolution symbol $(x*h)(t)$ inside the Fourier transform. The first move is to replace that symbol with its integral definition and leave the Fourier kernel $e^{-j\omega t}$ untouched.
Use the convolution definition $(x*h)(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$ and insert it directly into the transform integral.

After substitution, the transform becomes a nested integral with $t$ outside and $\tau$ inside. That is the whole move in this step: write the convolution inside the transform and stop before changing the order of integration.
No variables are changed yet, and the order of integration stays the same. The result is the substituted Fourier transform in a form that is ready for the next rewrite.

sections.lesson_title: Proof Idea of the Convolution Theorem
sections.section_title: Rewriting the Transform as an Iterated Integral

example_content.example_prompt: Rewrite the substituted Fourier transform as an iterated integral with respect to $\tau$ and $t$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the nested integral from the previous step. Keep the outer variable $t$ attached to the Fourier kernel $e^{-j\omega t}$ and rewrite the same expression so both integration variables are visible.
Now flatten that structure into a true iterated integral. The inner integral is still over $\tau$, and the outer integral is still over $t$; only the writing changes, not the algebra.
That is the entire move in this step: make the double-integral structure explicit so the next step can justify changing the order of integration.

sections.lesson_title: Proof Idea of the Convolution Theorem
sections.section_title: Interchanging the Order of Integration

example_content.example_prompt: Take the iterated integral for $Y(j\omega)$ and interchange the order of integration so the $t$-integral sits inside.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the double integral from the previous step. Keep the same integrand, but rewrite the expression so the $\tau$-integral is outside and the $t$-integral is inside.
Move $x(\tau)$ outside the inner $t$-integral and keep $h(t-\tau)e^{-j\omega t}$ inside. That is the only new wrinkle here: the structure changes, but the integrand does not.

The result is the same Fourier transform written in a form that isolates the shifted impulse response. No transform pair is recognized yet; this step only positions the inner integral for the next move.

sections.lesson_title: Proof Idea of the Convolution Theorem
sections.section_title: Exposing the Shifted Transform Factor

example_content.example_prompt: In the inner integral, make the substitution $u=t-\tau$ and expose the factor that carries the shift dependence.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the inner integral inside the swapped-order expression. Let $u=t-\tau$ so the shift moves off of $h$ and onto a clean exponential factor.
Replace $t$ by $u+\tau$ and $dt$ by $du$. Then $e^{-j\omega t}=e^{-j\omega(u+\tau)}=e^{-j\omega\tau}e^{-j\omega u}$, so the shift dependence separates.
The result is the shifted transform factor $e^{-j\omega\tau}H(j\omega)$, ready to be paired with the outer $x(\tau)$ integral in the next step.

sections.lesson_title: Proof Idea of the Convolution Theorem
sections.section_title: Recognizing the Product of the Two Individual Spectra

example_content.example_prompt: Recognize the separated factors in the transformed convolution expression and conclude that $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the separated factor form from the previous step. The outer integral over $\tau$ matches the Fourier transform of $x(t)$, and the remaining factor is $H(j\omega)$.
Name the outer integral $X(j\omega)$ and keep the transform factor $H(j\omega)$ as the multiplier that came out of the inner integral.
That finishes the proof idea: the convolution in time becomes multiplication in frequency, with each factor identified as the spectrum of one signal.

entries.lesson_title: Using the Convolution Theorem to Avoid Direct Convolution
entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a continuous-time LTI convolution problem into Fourier-domain multiplication by finding X(j\omega) and H(j\omega), simplifying Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega), and inverse-transforming to recover y(t).

sections.lesson_title: Using the Convolution Theorem to Avoid Direct Convolution
sections.section_title: Introduction to Using the Convolution Theorem to Avoid Direct Convolution

blocks.text: When an LTI output is written as $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$, the direct route is a convolution integral in $\tau$, and that can be the expensive part of the calculation. The shortcut in this section is to move the work into the Fourier domain instead of expanding the integral by hand.

The convolution theorem says the transform of the output is $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$. So the action to remember is simple: find the Fourier transforms of $x(t)$ and $h(t)$, multiply them to get $Y(j\omega)$, and treat that product as the frequency-domain version of the output.

In the simplest base case, both $x(t)$ and $h(t)$ already match standard transform pairs, so the only new move is to use the theorem-driven workflow instead of direct convolution. That means you stay in one stable notation all the way through the calculation: transform first, multiply second, and then return to $y(t)$ by inverse transforming the result.

Use this theorem whenever direct convolution is the bottleneck and the needed transform pairs are available. The result is a three-step shortcut you can reuse in later examples: transform the input and impulse response, multiply in frequency, and inverse-transform the product to recover $y(t)$.

sections.lesson_title: Using the Convolution Theorem to Avoid Direct Convolution
sections.section_title: Translating a Convolution Output into Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)

example_content.example_prompt: A system output is defined by $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$. Write the frequency-domain relation that lets you replace direct convolution with multiplication.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the output is already written as a convolution of the input and impulse response. For an LTI system, that is the signal to move into the Fourier domain and translate the convolution into a product.

So the frequency-domain relation is written with the output spectrum $Y(j\omega)$ on the left and the two factor spectra on the right. The input becomes $X(j\omega)$, the impulse response becomes $H(j\omega)$, and the theorem tells you to multiply them.

That is the translation to remember in this section: when the output is presented as a time-domain convolution, the matching frequency-domain statement is the product $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$. No extra algebra is needed yet; the task is only to identify the correct transform-domain form.

sections.lesson_title: Using the Convolution Theorem to Avoid Direct Convolution
sections.section_title: Finding X(j\omega) and H(j\omega) from Transform Pairs

example_content.example_prompt: Given simple standard-pair signals $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$, determine $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$ and set up the product for $Y(j\omega)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that both time-domain signals are one-sided decaying exponentials. That means you should not derive their Fourier transforms from scratch; you should match each signal to the standard transform pair for $e^{-at}u(t)$.

Apply that pair separately to each signal. For $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$, the parameter is $a=1$, so the input transform is $X(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega}$. For $h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$, the parameter is $a=2$, so the impulse-response transform is $H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{2+j\omega}$.

Now write the output spectrum as the product of those two transforms. The notation stays aligned with the theorem: $X(j\omega)$ comes from $x(t)$, $H(j\omega)$ comes from $h(t)$, and $Y(j\omega)$ is their product.

That is the full move in this step: recognize the standard pair, identify each transform correctly, and set up the frequency-domain product without simplifying it yet. The next step can work with the product itself.

sections.lesson_title: Using the Convolution Theorem to Avoid Direct Convolution
sections.section_title: Simplifying the Frequency-Domain Product Y(j\omega)

example_content.example_prompt: Given $X(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega}$ and $H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{2+j\omega}$, simplify $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ into a form ready for inverse transformation.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is the product from the previous step. The job is algebraic cleanup, not a new theorem: multiply the known transforms and rewrite the result so it matches a familiar inverse-transform shape.
Because the denominator is a product of two first-order terms, split it into a sum of simple pieces. That puts each term in a standard form you can invert directly in the next step.
This is the simplified frequency-domain form to keep: the same output spectrum, but now written as a sum of standard transform-pair terms. It is ready for the last time-domain step.

sections.lesson_title: Using the Convolution Theorem to Avoid Direct Convolution
sections.section_title: Inverse-Transforming Y(j\omega) to Recover y(t)

example_content.example_prompt: Given the simplified frequency-domain output $Y(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega}-\frac{1}{2+j\omega}$, use inverse-transform pairs to recover the time-domain signal $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the simplified spectrum from the previous step. The job now is recognition: match each term in $Y(j\omega)$ to a standard inverse-transform pair and then use linearity to return to the time domain.
Each denominator already matches the pair with $a=1$ and $a=2$. Apply the inverse transform term by term, keeping the minus sign attached to the second term.
That is the recovered time-domain output. The frequency-domain expression has been converted back into a clean causal signal by matching the inverse pair and preserving the algebra exactly.

sections.lesson_title: Using the Convolution Theorem to Avoid Direct Convolution
sections.section_title: Applying the Full Shortcut to an LTI System Output

example_content.example_prompt: For a complete continuous-time LTI problem with $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$, find the output $y(t)$ using the convolution theorem instead of evaluating the convolution integral.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a complete continuous-time LTI output problem, so the shortcut should carry the whole workflow. Start by moving out of the time-domain convolution and into the Fourier domain, because the theorem lets you replace the integral with multiplication.

Both signals match the standard one-sided exponential pair, so read off their spectra directly instead of deriving them from scratch. That gives the input transform and the impulse-response transform in the same notation used in the earlier steps.

Now multiply the factors and simplify the product into a form that is easy to invert. Because the denominator is a product of first-order terms, split it into simple inverse-pair terms rather than leaving it in unsimplified form.
The final step is to invert each term and keep the minus sign attached to the second component. This returns the time-domain output directly without ever evaluating the convolution integral.

That is the complete shortcut: transform the input and impulse response, multiply in frequency, simplify the product, and invert back to the output. The example shows the entire workflow in one pass so the same sequence can be reused on new LTI problems.
